transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I’m here because I’ve been getting really stuck on how my face looks, especially around my jaw. It’s like this sagging, uneven look on one side of my face that I can’t stop noticing.

It got worse after I saw myself in a bunch of family photos. Everyone else seemed to think the pictures were fine, but I kept zooming in and looking at my jawline and the side of my face, thinking, “Is that really how I look?” My wife tells me she barely notices anything, and even clients don’t seem to react or anything, but I still feel like it’s obvious. I know that probably sounds like a small thing, but it’s been hard for me to let it go once I see it.
How much does this concern about your jawline interfere with your daily life or cause you distress?

It does interfere, yeah… I mean, I’m still functioning, I still go to work and I’m not, like, staying in bed all day or anything. I’m a financial advisor, so I have to meet people and be put together, and I do get through the meetings. But it’s been slowing me down more than I’d like to admit.

Like before client appointments, especially if I know it’s in person, I’ll spend too long checking how my face looks from different angles, trying to see if the jaw thing is noticeable in the mirror or on my phone camera. And then I end up leaving later than I planned, or I’m kind of rushed and already tense by the time I get there.

During some appointments, I can still do my job, but I’m not as present as I should be. Part of my mind is on whether they’re looking at that side of my face, or whether the lighting is making it worse. I’ll catch myself thinking about my jaw when I should be fully listening.

And socially, I’ve skipped a few art openings. My wife and I sometimes go to those, and there are always people taking pictures, posting things, that kind of thing. I just didn’t want to be seen or photographed. I told myself I was tired or busy, but really it was because I didn’t want to deal with how I might look. It’s not ruining everything, but it’s definitely taking up space in my life.
When you’re worried about how your jaw looks, do you find yourself doing things like checking mirrors, taking pictures, or comparing your face to others repeatedly?

Yeah… I do. More than I really want to admit, honestly.

Before client meetings is when it’s probably the most obvious. I’ll go into the bathroom and check the mirror, then I’ll use my phone camera because somehow the mirror doesn’t feel like enough. And then I’ll check again from a slightly different angle, like turning my head a little to see if that side of my jaw looks more uneven. Sometimes I’ll mess with the lighting too, like step closer to the overhead light or away from it, because I’m trying to figure out if it’s just bad lighting or if that’s really how it looks.

And it’s not just checking once. It can be several times before I leave. I’ll adjust my collar, or try to position my face a certain way, like maybe if my shirt sits differently it draws less attention to it. Which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels important.

And yeah, I compare too. If I’m around other advisors, especially younger guys, I notice their jawlines or how their faces look more… firm, I guess. At gallery events too, I’ll catch myself looking at other people’s faces instead of just having a normal conversation. I’ll be standing there nodding along, but part of me is thinking, “His face looks normal, mine probably looks off.” It’s distracting, and then I feel embarrassed that I’m even doing it.

Do you find yourself repeating certain behaviors or thoughts over and over again when you’re concerned about your jawline, like checking multiple times, trying to fix it mentally, or going over it again and again in your head?

Yeah, definitely. It becomes this whole loop, especially before I’m about to see clients in person. I’ll tell myself, “Okay, just check once and go,” but then I end up in the bathroom looking in the mirror, turning my head slightly one way and then the other, trying to see if the jaw looks uneven or saggy from that side.

And then the mirror doesn’t feel reliable enough, so I’ll pull out my phone camera and check that too. Sometimes I’ll move closer to the light or step back, or tilt my face, because I’m trying to figure out if it’s the lighting making it look worse or if that’s just how I actually look. Then I’ll adjust my collar, maybe try to hold my face at a certain angle, like somehow that’s going to make it less noticeable.

And even after I leave, it keeps going in my head. If I’m with younger advisors or at a gallery event, I’ll catch myself comparing my face to theirs instead of paying attention to what’s being said. I’ll be nodding along, but mentally I’m thinking, “His jaw looks normal,” or “I wonder if mine looks worse from this angle.” It’s embarrassing, because I know I should just be focused on the conversation, but my mind keeps going back to it.
Have you ever avoided certain situations, like social events or even work-related activities, because you were so concerned about how your jawline looks?

Yeah, I have. Not constantly, but enough that it bothers me.

Work-wise, I don’t usually outright cancel client meetings because of it—I still go, I still do my job—but it affects the whole lead-up. I’ll get stuck checking my face before I leave, and then suddenly I’m running behind or I’m leaving the house tense and irritated with myself. So I’m technically showing up, but not in the calm, prepared way I’d like to. And during some appointments I can tell I’m not fully there, because part of me is still worrying about whether the client is noticing my jaw or how I look from their side of the table.

Socially, I’ve avoided more. My wife and I sometimes go to art openings, and I’ve skipped a few because I just didn’t want to be seen, or photographed, or end up in someone’s post looking bad. I usually give some normal excuse, like I’m tired or I have work to catch up on, but if I’m being honest, it’s really because I don’t want to deal with feeling exposed like that.

So it’s not like I’ve stopped living my life, but yes, I do avoid some things, and even when I don’t avoid them, it slows me down and takes me out of the moment.

When you're concerned about how your jawline looks, do you find yourself doing things over and over again — like checking your appearance, adjusting your posture, or trying to mentally 'fix' how you think you look — in order to feel reassured or to prevent something bad from happening?

Yes… I do. It’s not just a quick glance and then I move on. It turns into this whole routine, especially before client meetings.

I’ll go into the bathroom and check the mirror, and then I’ll think, “Well, maybe that angle isn’t accurate,” so I’ll pull out my phone camera and look there too. Then I’ll turn my head a little, check one side, then the other side, and I’ll mess with the lighting—like move closer to the overhead light or step back—because I’m trying to decide if my jaw really looks off or if it’s just shadows making it look worse.

And then I’ll start adjusting things, like my collar or the way my shirt sits, almost like if I can frame my face differently it won’t stand out as much. Sometimes I’ll kind of hold my face or posture a certain way, which is hard to explain without sounding strange, but in the moment it feels like I’m trying to make it look more normal before I go in front of people.

The mental part keeps going too. If I’m around younger advisors, or at gallery events, I’ll catch myself comparing my face to theirs instead of actually listening. I’ll be looking at someone’s jawline or profile and thinking, “Okay, his looks normal, mine probably doesn’t,” and then I’m trying to reassure myself or figure out how bad mine looks. It’s embarrassing, because I know I’m supposed to be focused on the conversation, but my mind keeps circling back to it.
Do you ever feel anxious or fearful in situations where people might be paying attention to you, even if it's not about how your face looks?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I can get a little tense if I’m “on,” like if I’m speaking with clients or I know people are looking to me to explain something clearly, but I’ve always thought of that as pretty normal work pressure.

It’s hard for me to separate it out, honestly. If people are paying attention to me, my mind usually goes pretty quickly to how I’m coming across physically, so I don’t know if I’m anxious about attention in general or if it just gets tied up with that. Like, if someone is listening closely, I’m not usually thinking, “They’re judging my personality” or “I’m going to embarrass myself.” It’s more… I become aware that I’m being seen.

So, outside of the appearance piece, I don’t know that I’ve noticed a big fear of attention by itself. I can do meetings, I can talk to people, I can handle being in a professional role. It’s just when that attention makes me feel visible that I start getting uncomfortable.
Outside of concerns about your appearance, do you ever feel anxious or self-conscious in social situations, like meeting new people or being the center of attention?

I don’t think so, not in a clear way. I mean, meeting new people can be a little awkward at first, but I don’t usually feel afraid of it on its own. If I’m introduced to someone at a work thing or a dinner or one of my wife’s art events, I can make conversation. I might be a bit stiff at the beginning, but I don’t think I’m sitting there worrying that I’ll say something humiliating or that they’ll dislike me as a person.

Being the center of attention is… I don’t love it, exactly, but I can handle it. Like if I have to explain something to clients or speak in a small group, I can do that. I may feel pressure to sound competent, but that feels different from social anxiety, I guess. It’s more like I want to do my job well.

So outside of the appearance part, I haven’t really noticed a separate pattern where I avoid people or panic about social situations. It’s more that if attention is on me, I become aware of being looked at, and then it can turn into that other thing. But just meeting people or talking to people, no, not really in itself.
When you're in situations where you feel others might be noticing how you look, does it cause you a lot of anxiety or distress, even if they’re not directly commenting on your appearance?

Yes, it does. I mean, even if no one says anything, that’s almost what makes it worse sometimes, because then I’m trying to read their faces and figure out whether they noticed.

What really brought me in is that I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face. It started feeling much more real to me after I saw myself in a bunch of family photos. I know photos can catch you at bad angles, and my wife tells me she barely notices anything, and clients obviously aren’t saying anything about it… but in my head it feels obvious. Like if I’m sitting across from someone, I’ll think, “They can see that side of my face looks lower,” or “My jawline looks soft and uneven,” and then I get really tense.

It’s not that people are commenting directly. They usually aren’t. That’s part of why I feel a little ridiculous explaining it. But I still feel distressed because I’m convinced they might be noticing it silently. My wife will say, “You look fine,” or “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” and I want to believe her, but it doesn’t really settle it for me. It just keeps coming back, especially if I’m in a situation where I feel visible.
Do you believe that the issue with your jawline is something that others would notice and judge, or do you think it's something that really isn't obvious to anyone but you?

I go back and forth, but if I’m being honest, in the moment it feels like other people could notice it. Like the sagging or unevenness around my jawline and one side of my face feels so obvious to me once I’ve locked onto it that I have a hard time believing no one else can see it.

At the same time, I know that sounds… maybe not completely logical, because my wife says she barely sees what I’m talking about, and clients don’t comment on it or seem to react in any obvious way. But that doesn’t really reassure me for long. I’ll think, well, maybe they’re just being polite, or maybe they notice but wouldn’t say anything because that would be rude.

It really got worse after I saw myself in those family photos. I kept seeing this sagging, uneven look, especially around the jaw and one side of my face, and now it’s like I can’t unsee it. So part of me knows it might not be obvious to everyone else, or maybe not as bad as I think, but the stronger feeling is that people probably do notice it and are just not saying anything.

When you think about your jawline looking uneven or sagging, does it feel like a flaw that makes you fear others will see you as unattractive or less capable, or does it feel more like a medical issue that something might be wrong with your face physically?

It feels more like an appearance flaw, I think. Not so much like I’m worried there’s a disease or something physically wrong with my face in a medical sense. It’s more that I get stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face, and then I start thinking that’s what people are seeing when they look at me.

What brings me in is really that I can’t seem to let it go, especially after seeing myself in all those family photos. I kept noticing the same thing over and over — the jawline looking softer, one side looking lower or not matching — and now it sort of jumps out at me. Even though my wife says she barely notices anything, and clients don’t say anything or act like they’re noticing, I still feel like it’s there.

So, yeah, it’s not that I think my face is medically damaged. It’s more that I worry it makes me look… I don’t know, older, unattractive, maybe less put-together than I want to seem. Like people might be taking me less seriously or silently judging me, even if they’re not saying it.
Do you spend a lot of time thinking about how your jawline looks, to the point where it’s hard to focus on other things, even when you try not to?

Yes… I do. Probably more than I want to admit. It’s like once the thought gets in my head, I keep circling back to it, even if I’m supposed to be paying attention to something else.

What really brings me in is that I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face. And it became a lot harder to ignore after I saw myself in all those family photos. I know people say photos can distort things, or catch you in a bad moment, but I kept seeing it again and again, and now it’s like my eye goes straight to that part of my face.

Even when my wife tells me she barely notices anything, or when I’m with clients and they don’t say anything about it, I still find myself thinking about it. I’ll be trying to focus on a conversation or work, and then part of my mind is off wondering how my jawline looks from that angle, whether one side looks lower, whether they can tell. I can still function, I guess, but it takes up more space in my head than it should.
Do you ever try to cover up or hide the appearance of your jawline, like adjusting your clothing, hairstyle, or using makeup or accessories, to make it less noticeable?

Yeah, I do, though I don’t know if I’d call it “covering up” exactly. It’s more like I try to manage how it’s seen, if that makes sense.

Before client meetings especially, I’ll stop in the bathroom and check the mirror, then sometimes I’ll pull out my phone camera too, because the mirror and the camera don’t always look the same to me. I’ll look from one side, then the other side, adjust the lighting if I can, tilt my head a little, almost like I’m trying to find the angle where the jawline doesn’t look as uneven or saggy. And then I’ll mess with my collar, like if my shirt or jacket sits a certain way maybe it distracts from it or frames my face better. It sounds kind of ridiculous saying it out loud, but I do it.

I don’t really use makeup or anything like that, but I definitely think about angles and lighting and how I’m holding my face. Sometimes in meetings or at gallery events, instead of just listening and being present, I’ll catch myself comparing my face to other people’s, especially younger advisors or younger-looking people there. I’ll be thinking, “Their jawline looks sharper,” or “They look more put together,” and then I’m half in the conversation and half stuck in my own head about my face.
Do you ever think that other people might also be worried about similar things with their faces, or does it feel like this is something specific to you?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, logically, yes, I know other people probably have things they don’t like about their faces. My wife will sometimes make a comment about a photo of herself or someone will joke about getting older, that kind of thing. So I know I’m not the only person who notices things.

But emotionally, when I’m in it, it feels very specific to me. Like other people might dislike a picture here or there and then move on, but for me it feels like this one thing on my jaw just… stands out. I don’t usually look at someone else and think, “Oh, they must be worried about their face too.” I’m more focused on whether they’re seeing mine.

I guess I haven’t really thought much about whether other people are going through the same kind of thing. It feels like they probably aren’t noticing themselves the way I’m noticing myself, if that makes sense. Or at least they don’t seem to be. They seem more comfortable just being in a room or having their picture taken, and I’m the one trying to figure out what angle I’m being seen from.

Do you feel that your concern about how your jawline looks consumes your thoughts so much that it interferes with your ability to enjoy life or perform daily tasks, even beyond the checking and adjusting you've described?

Yes… I mean, I still get through the day. I don’t want to make it sound like I can’t work or that everything has fallen apart, because that wouldn’t be true. I do my job, I meet with clients, I handle what I need to handle.

But it does interfere more than I’d like. Before client meetings, I’ve been slower getting out the door because I get caught checking how I look, or adjusting my collar, or looking at my face again before I leave. Sometimes I tell myself it’ll just take a second, and then suddenly I’ve lost ten or fifteen minutes and I’m annoyed with myself before the meeting even starts.

And during appointments, I can usually stay professional, but I’m not always fully present. Like part of me is listening to what the client is saying, and another part of me is wondering if they’re looking at that side of my face, or if the lighting in the room is making it worse. I don’t think clients would necessarily know, but I can feel that I’m not as focused as I should be.

The bigger thing socially is I’ve skipped a few art openings, which I used to enjoy. Not every time, but a few. If I thought there’d be photos or a lot of people I know, I just… didn’t want to be seen that way. I’d come up with some reason not to go, but really it was because I didn’t want to be standing around thinking about my jawline the whole time or worrying someone would take a picture. So yes, I guess it has started taking some of the enjoyment out of things.

F21 is ruled out due to less emphasis on delusional beliefs and more on appearance-related anxiety and compulsive behaviors consistent with somatic symptom or anxiety disorders.

Sometimes I’ll kind of hold my face or posture a certain way, which is hard to explain without sounding strange, but in the moment it feels like I’m trying to make it look more normal before I go in front of people.

The mental part keeps going too. If I’m around younger advisors, or at gallery events, I’ll catch myself comparing my face to theirs instead of actually listening. I’ll be looking at someone’s jawline or profile and thinking, “Okay, his looks normal, mine probably doesn’t,” and then I’m trying to reassure myself or figure out how bad mine looks. It’s embarrassing, because I know I’m supposed to be focused on the conversation, but my mind keeps circling back to it.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel anxious or fearful in situations where people might be paying attention to you, even if it's not about how your face looks?

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure. I mean, I can get a little tense if I’m “on,” like if I’m speaking with clients or I know people are looking to me to explain something clearly, but I’ve always thought of that as pretty normal work pressure.

It’s hard for me to separate it out, honestly. If people are paying attention to me, my mind usually goes pretty quickly to how I’m coming across physically, so I don’t know if I’m anxious about attention in general or if it just gets tied up with that. Like, if someone is listening closely, I’m not usually thinking, “They’re judging my personality” or “I’m going to embarrass myself.” It’s more… I become aware that I’m being seen.

So, outside of the appearance piece, I don’t know that I’ve noticed a big fear of attention by itself. I can do meetings, I can talk to people, I can handle being in a professional role. It’s just when that attention makes me feel visible that I start getting uncomfortable.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or avoidance in social situations beyond concerns about appearance, which would support a diagnosis of Social Anxiety Disorder (F40.10) or help distinguish it from Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22).

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not in a clear way. I mean, meeting new people can be a little awkward at first, but I don’t usually feel afraid of it on its own. If I’m introduced to someone at a work thing or a dinner or one of my wife’s art events, I can make conversation. I might be a bit stiff at the beginning, but I don’t think I’m sitting there worrying that I’ll say something humiliating or that they’ll dislike me as a person.

Being the center of attention is… I don’t love it, exactly, but I can handle it. Like if I have to explain something to clients or speak in a small group, I can do that. I may feel pressure to sound competent, but that feels different from social anxiety, I guess. It’s more like I want to do my job well.

So outside of the appearance part, I haven’t really noticed a separate pattern where I avoid people or panic about social situations. It’s more that if attention is on me, I become aware of being looked at, and then it can turn into that other thing. But just meeting people or talking to people, no, not really in itself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant anxiety or distress in response to perceived scrutiny by others related to their appearance, which would help distinguish between Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22) and Social Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).
doctor.question: When you're in situations where you feel others might be noticing how you look, does it cause you a lot of anxiety or distress, even if they’re not directly commenting on your appearance?

patient.answer:
Yes, it does. I mean, even if no one says anything, that’s almost what makes it worse sometimes, because then I’m trying to read their faces and figure out whether they noticed.

What really brought me in is that I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face. It started feeling much more real to me after I saw myself in a bunch of family photos. I know photos can catch you at bad angles, and my wife tells me she barely notices anything, and clients obviously aren’t saying anything about it… but in my head it feels obvious. Like if I’m sitting across from someone, I’ll think, “They can see that side of my face looks lower,” or “My jawline looks soft and uneven,” and then I get really tense.

It’s not that people are commenting directly. They usually aren’t. That’s part of why I feel a little ridiculous explaining it. But I still feel distressed because I’m convinced they might be noticing it silently. My wife will say, “You look fine,” or “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” and I want to believe her, but it doesn’t really settle it for me. It just keeps coming back, especially if I’m in a situation where I feel visible.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant preoccupation with a perceived or slight physical defect that is not observable to others, which is key to differentiating between the two remaining diagnoses (F45.22 - Body Dysmorphic Disorder and F41.1 - Generalized Anxiety Disorder).

patient.answer:
I go back and forth, but if I’m being honest, in the moment it feels like other people could notice it. Like the sagging or unevenness around my jawline and one side of my face feels so obvious to me once I’ve locked onto it that I have a hard time believing no one else can see it.

At the same time, I know that sounds… maybe not completely logical, because my wife says she barely sees what I’m talking about, and clients don’t comment on it or seem to react in any obvious way. But that doesn’t really reassure me for long. I’ll think, well, maybe they’re just being polite, or maybe they notice but wouldn’t say anything because that would be rude.

It really got worse after I saw myself in those family photos. I kept seeing this sagging, uneven look, especially around the jaw and one side of my face, and now it’s like I can’t unsee it. So part of me knows it might not be obvious to everyone else, or maybe not as bad as I think, but the stronger feeling is that people probably do notice it and are just not saying anything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concern about their jawline is better explained by a preoccupation with perceived physical defects (as in body dysmorphic disorder) rather than a more generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: When you think about your jawline looking uneven or sagging, does it feel like a flaw that makes you fear others will see you as unattractive or less capable, or does it feel more like a medical issue that something might be wrong with your face physically?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance

patient.answer:
It feels more like an appearance flaw, I think. Not so much like I’m worried there’s a disease or something physically wrong with my face in a medical sense. It’s more that I get stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face, and then I start thinking that’s what people are seeing when they look at me.

What brings me in is really that I can’t seem to let it go, especially after seeing myself in all those family photos. I kept noticing the same thing over and over — the jawline looking softer, one side looking lower or not matching — and now it sort of jumps out at me. Even though my wife says she barely notices anything, and clients don’t say anything or act like they’re noticing, I still feel like it’s there.

So, yeah, it’s not that I think my face is medically damaged. It’s more that I worry it makes me look… I don’t know, older, unattractive, maybe less put-together than I want to seem. Like people might be taking me less seriously or silently judging me, even if they’re not saying it.

doctor.question: Do you spend a lot of time thinking about how your jawline looks, to the point where it’s hard to focus on other things, even when you try not to?

patient.answer:
Yes… I do. Probably more than I want to admit. It’s like once the thought gets in my head, I keep circling back to it, even if I’m supposed to be paying attention to something else.

What really brings me in is that I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face. And it became a lot harder to ignore after I saw myself in all those family photos. I know people say photos can distort things, or catch you in a bad moment, but I kept seeing it again and again, and now it’s like my eye goes straight to that part of my face.

Even when my wife tells me she barely notices anything, or when I’m with clients and they don’t say anything about it, I still find myself thinking about it. I’ll be trying to focus on a conversation or work, and then part of my mind is off wondering how my jawline looks from that angle, whether one side looks lower, whether they can tell. I can still function, I guess, but it takes up more space in my head than it should.

doctor.question: Do you ever try to cover up or hide the appearance of your jawline, like adjusting your clothing, hairstyle, or using makeup or accessories, to make it less noticeable?

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do, though I don’t know if I’d call it “covering up” exactly. It’s more like I try to manage how it’s seen, if that makes sense.

Before client meetings especially, I’ll stop in the bathroom and check the mirror, then sometimes I’ll pull out my phone camera too, because the mirror and the camera don’t always look the same to me. I’ll look from one side, then the other side, adjust the lighting if I can, tilt my head a little, almost like I’m trying to find the angle where the jawline doesn’t look as uneven or saggy. And then I’ll mess with my collar, like if my shirt or jacket sits a certain way maybe it distracts from it or frames my face better. It sounds kind of ridiculous saying it out loud, but I do it.

I don’t really use makeup or anything like that, but I definitely think about angles and lighting and how I’m holding my face. Sometimes in meetings or at gallery events, instead of just listening and being present, I’ll catch myself comparing my face to other people’s, especially younger advisors or younger-looking people there. I’ll be thinking, “Their jawline looks sharper,” or “They look more put together,” and then I’m half in the conversation and half stuck in my own head about my face.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient believes their perceived facial flaw is unique to them or if they believe others have similar concerns.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure. I mean, logically, yes, I know other people probably have things they don’t like about their faces. My wife will sometimes make a comment about a photo of herself or someone will joke about getting older, that kind of thing. So I know I’m not the only person who notices things.

But emotionally, when I’m in it, it feels very specific to me. Like other people might dislike a picture here or there and then move on, but for me it feels like this one thing on my jaw just… stands out. I don’t usually look at someone else and think, “Oh, they must be worried about their face too.” I’m more focused on whether they’re seeing mine.

I guess I haven’t really thought much about whether other people are going through the same kind of thing. It feels like they probably aren’t noticing themselves the way I’m noticing myself, if that makes sense. Or at least they don’t seem to be. They seem more comfortable just being in a room or having their picture taken, and I’m the one trying to figure out what angle I’m being seen from.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, I still get through the day. I don’t want to make it sound like I can’t work or that everything has fallen apart, because that wouldn’t be true. I do my job, I meet with clients, I handle what I need to handle.

But it does interfere more than I’d like. Before client meetings, I’ve been slower getting out the door because I get caught checking how I look, or adjusting my collar, or looking at my face again before I leave. Sometimes I tell myself it’ll just take a second, and then suddenly I’ve lost ten or fifteen minutes and I’m annoyed with myself before the meeting even starts.

And during appointments, I can usually stay professional, but I’m not always fully present. Like part of me is listening to what the client is saying, and another part of me is wondering if they’re looking at that side of my face, or if the lighting in the room is making it worse. I don’t think clients would necessarily know, but I can feel that I’m not as focused as I should be.

The bigger thing socially is I’ve skipped a few art openings, which I used to enjoy. Not every time, but a few. If I thought there’d be photos or a lot of people I know, I just… didn’t want to be seen that way. I’d come up with some reason not to go, but really it was because I didn’t want to be standing around thinking about my jawline the whole time or worrying someone would take a picture. So yes, I guess it has started taking some of the enjoyment out of things.
